claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and picks the best one for each geo.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, and GeoDeploy will not run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.

Jev exposes three primitives: choice(), which returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence; score(), which rates against a rubric; and noul(), which answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
GeoDeploy's score() rubrics use 10 levels.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates.
GeoDeploy asks Jev in a single call for a selection, five quality scores, two hard checks (residency and capacity), and a fallback region.
The code sample is from packages/decide/src/questions.ts and imports choice, noul, score from @typesafe-ai/sdk.
TypeSafe advises to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing rubrics.
The TypeSafeClient has a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers with selection.choice, confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Weights can be re-tuned without calling Jev again because they live in code.
Weight profiles have specific values, e.g. latency-optimized: cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow from the provider, and Jev decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); new-cluster region 0.90 (top three flagged for human); existing-stack region 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
The residency check is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers) so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic price comparison across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

Self-driving mode is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`; the agent periodically checks CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, shift:<from>-><to>, plus a disruption risk check.

In self-driving mode, code rather than Jev computes node-count changes; above 0.85 confidence resize is applied automatically, between 0.70 and 0.85 suggested for human approval, below 0.70 falls back to a deterministic per-region rule.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency and error rates.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API page exists at /automation/.
Pulumi Automation API docs exist at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
In GeoDeploy the TypeScript app does the math, Jev decides region and modules and never does arithmetic or generates code, and Pulumi provisions and decides nothing.
